data.description:
## Depends on - **MRQ-171** must be merged first. It extracts the theme switcher into one shared component in `src/ui/shell/`, and this ticket consumes that component rather than writing a third copy. - The uncommitted `PortalPage.tsx` work in flight on 2026-08-13 (organizer-with-no- speaker-seat dead end, comms send disclosures, reversal counts) must be merged first. **Rebase on `github/main` and confirm those changes are present before you start**, or you will resolve conflicts in the most-seen surface in the product. ## Part 1 — a speaker with several talks The arrival math is already right, and it is better than it looks. `arrivalForSession` in `src/lib/venue-geometry.ts` picks the speaker's **own** most recent same-day session that ends before this one starts, and computes the walk from *that* building. A speaker with a 10:00 in the Sheraton and a 14:30 in the Workshop Annex already gets a leave-by that accounts for the walk between their own two talks. **Do not touch that math.** It is correct, it is shared with mail and ICS, and it has a test suite. The presentation is what fails. Three defects and one missing idea. **1a · The order is wrong.** `src/routes/portal.routes.ts:755` selects a speaker's submissions `ORDER BY s.updated_at DESC, s.id ASC` — edit recency. Two accepted talks therefore render in whatever order they were last touched, not the order the speaker will give them. The chain is computed correctly and then displayed out of sequence: the portal can show talk #2's arrival plan above talk #1's. Order scheduled submissions by their slot start; keep a deterministic tail for unscheduled ones so the list never flickers between loads. **1b · Duplicate DOM ids.** `ArrivalCard` keys both `id` and `aria-labelledby` on `slot.starts_at` (`portal-arrival-${starts_at}`, `arrival-heading-${starts_at}`). Two participations at the same instant emit the same id twice, and a screen reader follows the first. This is reachable in the seeded demo data, not theoretical — the seed deliberately guarantees live double-bookings so the `person` conflict class fires. Key on `submission.id`. **1c · The `index === 0` framing does not survive several talks.** The first hero reads "Current status" in an `

`, the rest "Submission status". That is a single-submission framing. Re-word so a speaker with three talks reads something true. **1d · Nothing states the movement — build the day strip.** This is the substance of the ticket. When a speaker has **more than one scheduled session**, render a compact day strip above the talk cards: ``` YOUR CONFERENCE DAY · Tue Oct 13 ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 10:00 Shipping agents that don't lie │ │ Metropolitan Ballroom │ │ Sheraton · be in by 9:45 │ │ │ │ │ │ 18 min walk · + 5 min to get in │ │ │ leave by 14:07 │ │ │ │ │ 14:30 The eval trap │ │ Workshop Annex │ │ 41 Madison Ave · side entrance │ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ [ one map, both pins ] ``` Sessions in time order; the movement between them as the connective tissue. Every number in it already exists in the portal payload (`slot.location`, `slot.arrival.walk_minutes`, `access_minutes`, `leave_by`, `previous_session`). **Add no new arithmetic** — if a number you want is not in the payload, widen the payload from the existing projection rather than recomputing anything client-side. - **One map, not N.** The strip carries a single `VenueMap` with a pin per distinct building. The repeated per-talk maps collapse into it. The per-talk cards keep their detail (room, address, getting in, entry time, arrival plan) below, in the same order. - **It folds.** A speaker with one scheduled session sees exactly what they see today — no strip. This mirrors the venue disclosure rule already in the product: venue surfaces show for every conference but fold when there is one building. - **Multiple days.** A speaker with sessions on two days gets one group per day, in order, each with its own date heading. Movement is only ever computed within a day — which is already how `previousSessionFor` behaves, so follow it rather than inventing an overnight leg. - **Degrade honestly.** Say what is true when it is not ready: an unplaced session, a building with no map pin, a room whose building is unassigned. The existing `arrival.status` vocabulary (`ready` / `unscheduled` / `unassigned` / `unavailable`) already distinguishes these and the current copy says the right thing for each — reuse those sentences, do not write new ones that contradict them. - **Same building, consecutive talks:** no walk leg, and do not print "0 min walk". Say the room changes, or say nothing. ## Part 2 — the seat chrome contract Both non-admin seats get the two affordances the organizer already has. **2a · The brand mark navigates to your seat home.** `src/ui/portal/PortalPage.tsx`'s `Marquee · Speaker portal` and `src/ui/portal/CoSpeakerPage.tsx`'s equivalent are plain spans — not links, not clickable. Make each a real link to that seat's home, sourced from the helper MRQ-171 put in `src/lib/auth/signin-destination.ts`, not a hardcoded second copy of the role→home mapping. Every error and loading branch of `PortalPage` renders its own copy of the topline (there are at least five) — fix them all, or better, render one topline component and delete the duplicates. **2b · The theme switcher.** The theme system is global and already correct — `html[data-theme]`, `localStorage`, the pre-paint script in `index.html` — so a theme chosen elsewhere already persists onto the portal. What is missing is the control. Drop in the shared component MRQ-171 created. **Do not write another switcher**; there were two copies before MRQ-171 and the point of the extraction was to stop at one. ## Acceptance criteria 1. A speaker with two scheduled sessions in different buildings sees the day strip, in time order, with the walk and leave-by between them stated once. 2. A speaker with one scheduled session sees no strip and a portal otherwise unchanged from today. 3. A speaker with sessions on two days sees one group per day; no movement leg is drawn across a night. 4. Exactly one map renders for a multi-talk speaker, with one pin per distinct building. 5. Submissions render in the order the speaker will give them, not `updated_at` order, and the order is stable across reloads. 6. No duplicate DOM ids for a speaker with two participations at the same instant. Verify against the seeded double-booking, not a hand-built fixture. 7. Unplaced, unpinned, and building-unassigned sessions each read honestly in the strip, using the existing `arrival.status` copy. 8. Clicking "Marquee" on the portal and on the co-speaker page lands on that seat's home, from a cold-opened tab, in every branch of the page including the error and loading states. 9. The theme switcher is present and functional on both, the choice persists across a reload and across navigation to another seat, and exactly one implementation of the control exists in the codebase. 10. Elements never jump: the strip must not shift when a leave-by resolves or a count changes. Tabular numerals for times and durations, reserved height for the arrival line. 11. Usable at 375px — the strip is the surface most likely to be read on a phone at a conference, so treat mobile as the primary case here rather than an afterthought. ## Do not - Do not change `arrivalForSession`, `previousSessionFor`, or `walkingMinutes`. The geometry is shared with mail and ICS, and it is right. - Do not compute a leave-by, a walk, or an entry allowance in the component. - Do not replace the per-talk status heroes wholesale. Replacing them with one day plan was considered and deliberately deferred: it touches the participation confirm/decline actions and is a rewrite of the portal's most-seen surface. The strip sits above them. - Do not add a theme switcher implementation. ## Validation Drive it. Local dev needs `--var INSECURE_LOCAL_COOKIES:1` or WKWebView and Safari drop the `Secure` session cookie on `http://` and every request 401s in the browser only, while curl passes. Find a seeded speaker with two accepted talks in different buildings and open their portal — if the seed has none, that is itself a finding worth reporting, because it means this whole path is inert in the demo. Then check: one talk, two talks same building, two talks different buildings, two days, an unplaced session, and the seeded double-booking. Screenshots of the strip at desktop and 375px in the PR.
data.title: The speaker portal shows a set of talks, not a day — plus the seat chrome contract

provenance.reason: Operator ruling 2026-08-13: day strip for multi-talk speakers; brand mark and theme switcher on every signed-in seat

data.body:
SEED FINDING — read this before you start, it changes the shape of the work.

The day strip's headline case does not exist in the seeded demo data. I checked scripts/seed/agenda.ts rather than assuming.

What the seed DOES guarantee: two pairs of accepted sessions 'begin together in different rooms' (agenda.ts:117-123) — starts[] is [13:00, 13:00, 14:00, 14:00] on day two — and addConflictParticipation() attaches the lead speaker of submission A onto submission B as a moderator. The first pair deliberately crosses Sheraton to Marriott so a live Transit conflict fires. So there IS a seeded person holding two sessions in two different buildings.

But both of that person's sessions start at the SAME INSTANT. That gives you:

- AC-6 (duplicate DOM ids) reproduces exactly as written. Good — verify against this person, not a hand-built fixture.
- The SEQUENTIAL case does not exist. previousSessionFor() only matches a session whose start + duration <= the current start, so for two simultaneous sessions neither is the other's previous and both fall back to primaryBuilding. There is no seeded speaker anywhere with a 10:00 in one building and a 14:30 in another.

Which means: the walk-between-your-own-talks leg — the one thing the strip is being built to say — would render for nobody in the demo. Green tests, dead feature. That is the exact trap this project has already been bitten by twice (the venue coordinates seeding both buildings at identical lat/lng, and AC-244 proven against a hand-built fixture over empty real data).

So the ticket grows by one item, and it is not optional:

**Seed a speaker with two sequential sessions in different buildings on the same day**, far enough apart that a real leave-by falls out of the geometry, and close enough that the walk matters. Same discipline as MRQ-62's Transit fix: check:seed should fail if that speaker stops existing. Reuse an existing accepted submission and an existing person rather than inflating the accepted count — reset-demo has a baseline cardinality contract that the seed comments call out explicitly, so do not add rows casually.

Also worth knowing: the conflict participation is seeded with role 'moderator', not speaker. Confirm the portal's submission list includes participations where the person is a moderator before you build on top of it — if it does not, the seeded conflict person has a one-talk portal and none of this is reachable from the portal at all.

GATE DISCIPLINE — binding for whoever implements this ticket. Inherited from the merge captain's fleet instruction, 2026-08-13.

Route EVERY pr-gate and EVERY full npm test through the shared box-wide lock:

  /Users/atin/Projects/Stage11/deployments/Marquee-worktrees/.gate-lock/gate-lock.sh npm run pr-gate -- --ticket MRQ-174
  /Users/atin/Projects/Stage11/deployments/Marquee-worktrees/.gate-lock/gate-lock.sh npm test

No exceptions, including one-off 'just checking' runs. Cheap scoped things — tsc, a single test file, check:design — stay unlocked and should NOT take the lock.

WHY, because the reason changes how you read your own results. Eval Triage measured the same branch at 78s under load 14 and 276s under load 164, against a 120s budget. Load on this box has swung 14 to 164 in a single evening with six local Workers up. An unserialized gate on a loaded box tells you nothing.

Know exactly what the lock buys you: 'no two PARTICIPATING gates overlap.' It is mkdir-based, reaps a dead owner's lock, prints the load it acquired at, and releases on exit/INT/TERM. It does NOT hold the box quiet — nothing makes a non-participant wait. So still check uptime before you believe a red.

THREE RULES THAT TRAVEL WITH IT:

1. A timeout and a red are indistinguishable in an unserialized run. If your only evidence for a defect is 'it timed out', you have no evidence. Re-run under the lock before you believe it, and never report a timeout as a failing test.

2. CI fast-gate is the trustworthy oracle, because it runs on GitHub's box where local load was never a factor. Where CI and a local run disagree about TIMING, CI is right. That does not extend to correctness — if CI is green and you find a real defect by reading the code, your finding wins.

3. Timing-independent evidence survives contention and does not need the lock or a re-run: typechecks, static checks, trace:ac, check:design, check:api, and any read of the diff. Only wall-clock-sensitive results need re-running.

ALSO STANDING WHEN YOU PICK THIS UP — verify the freeze state before assuming it: round 9 auto-eval grading was live on 2026-08-13 with .deploy-freeze set. Under that freeze, merging is fine and DEPLOYING is not: no wrangler deploy, no re-deploying the same sha (it re-seeds demo D1 under a running browse), no rm of .deploy-freeze, no running sequence/auto-eval/loop.sh barrier, no live D1 migrations. check:deploy reading 'frozen — do not deploy' is the marker working, not a gate failure to force past. Check whether the freeze still holds before you act on any of this — it may well have lifted by the time this ticket is dispatched.

One caution specific to this ticket: sequence/auto-eval/README.md claims a serialization guarantee that loop.sh declares (GATE_LOCK, line 24) and never calls — zero call sites. Do not trust that README. The wrapper above is the only real serialization. It is the same failure shape as the seed finding in the comment above this one and the 'pre-existing' typecheck claim on PR #199: correct-looking, silently absent. Grep for the call site before you trust a documented guarantee.

HOW TO TEST THIS TICKET — the day strip is UI-heavy and there is no DOM harness in this repo. Established while building MRQ-171, 2026-08-13. Read this before you plan your tests, not after.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST
No jsdom, no happy-dom, no @testing-library, no preact/test-utils. vitest.node.config.ts sets environment "node". You cannot mount a component, click, hover, or drive a state transition in a unit test. Nothing in this repo can.

WHAT THE PROJECT ACTUALLY USES
preact-render-to-string. See tests/unit/submitter-seat.MRQ-154.test.ts: import h from preact and renderToString, build typed fixture props, render the real component, assert on the emitted HTML. That is the pattern here.

E2E IS A DECLARED GAP, NOT AN OPTION. playwright.config.ts points testDir at ./tests/e2e, which does not exist. scripts/checks/run-e2e.mjs handles that honestly — it emits a stub naming owner MRQ-50, reason "the deployed 11-step Playwright loop has not landed", and the replacement instruction. If MRQ-50 has landed by the time you read this, e2e IS your best tool for the day strip and you should use it. Check before assuming either way.

DO NOT ADD A TEST DEPENDENCY to make this easier. BUILDPLAN section 7 reserves package.json and package-lock.json to M-06 through the orchestrator, and a new vitest environment is not a side quest for a UI ticket.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE DAY STRIP'S DESIGN

Make the strip a pure function of its props. Given the portal payload — submissions with slot.location, slot.arrival (walk_minutes, access_minutes, leave_by, previous_session, status) and the event timezone — the strip's entire output should be derivable at first render with no effects, no fetches of its own, and no state that only exists after an interaction. The ticket already forbids computing any arithmetic client-side, which points the same way.

Do that and every acceptance criterion in this ticket becomes testable with renderToString:

- AC-1 two sessions, different buildings: assert both titles, both times, the walk leg and the leave-by all appear, in time order in the emitted HTML.
- AC-2 one session: assert no strip element is emitted at all.
- AC-3 two days: assert two day groups and NO movement leg spanning them.
- AC-4 one map, one pin per distinct building: assert the count of pin elements.
- AC-5 ordering: feed submissions deliberately out of slot order and assert the rendered order is by slot time. This is the one most likely to pass by accident if your fixture is already sorted — shuffle it on purpose.
- AC-6 duplicate DOM ids: render a speaker with two participations at the SAME starts_at and assert the emitted id attributes are unique. This is a string assertion on the HTML and it is a real one, because the defect is literally a duplicated id in the output.
- AC-7 unplaced / unpinned / building-unassigned: one render per arrival.status value, asserting the existing copy for each.
- AC-10 elements never jump: partially checkable — assert the reserved-height container and the tabular-numeral class are present whether or not leave_by resolved.

What renderToString CANNOT prove, and which therefore needs the browser drive the ticket already requires: 375px layout, actual non-jumping under a state change, and map tiles rendering. Name those explicitly in the PR as covered-by-drive rather than covered-by-test.

THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST, and it is why this comment exists. MRQ-171 shipped a green PR in which an existing contract test had been amended to assert that STRINGS EXIST rather than that the PATH WORKS — so a whole feature (MRQ-169's revision surface) was orphaned and the suite stayed green. It was caught by a human-equivalent reading, not by any gate.

So: a test that asserts a label is present is not a test of a feature. If part of this ticket genuinely cannot be covered with the tooling available, DECLARE the gap explicitly in the PR body and name what is uncovered — in the style of run-e2e.mjs's stub, which states its owner, its reason and its replacement. An honest declared gap is acceptable. Coverage that looks real and is not is the thing that costs.

And write every new test so you have SEEN IT FAIL for the right reason before the fix lands. A test that has never been red is not evidence.

CORRECTING MY OWN SEED FINDING ABOVE — the conclusion survives, the reasoning did not, and the corrected version tells you exactly how to fix it cheaply with real data.

WHAT I SAID EARLIER: "There is no seeded speaker anywhere with a 10:00 in one building and a 14:30 in another."

WHAT I HAD ACTUALLY CHECKED: only the two deliberately-seeded conflict pairs in agenda.ts, which start simultaneously. I reasoned from those to a claim about every speaker in the seed, and I noted at the time that a repeat speaker from the real 2025 program was "possible but not guaranteed" — then stated the negative anyway. That is proving existence and calling it reachability, in reverse: I proved the conflict pairs could not produce a sequence and concluded nothing else could either.

WHAT I HAVE NOW VERIFIED, against sequence/research/sources/aie-summit-2025-program.json and the seed modules:

- The source has 60 speaker-bearing sessions and 75 distinct speakers, of whom exactly TWO appear in more than one session: Beyang Liu and Alex Volkov, twice each.
- accepted-core.ts keys people by NAME (person_id: ids.get(speaker.name)), so a repeat speaker is one person row with two participations on two different submissions. The mechanism for a multi-talk speaker exists and is live.
- Their sessions sit at accepted-order indices — Beyang Liu 6 and 32; Alex Volkov 24 and 47.
- agenda.ts schedules only accepted.slice(0, 24), i.e. indices 0 through 23, and only those rows get agenda_items.
- Module order is event, acceptedCore, pool, evaluations, submissionContent, agenda (src/lib/reset-demo/seed-modules.ts), and pool.ts creates no accepted rows, so accepted-core's insertion order is the index order agenda.ts slices.

CONCLUSION, now actually established rather than inferred: no speaker has two SCHEDULED sessions. Beyang Liu has exactly one inside the window (index 6, the other at 32); Alex Volkov has none (24 and 47 both fall outside a 0..23 slice). So the day strip would still render for nobody, and the original finding stands.

WHY THE CORRECTED VERSION IS WORTH MORE THAN THE ORIGINAL: it names the cheap fix, using real source data instead of fabrication.

Beyang Liu ALREADY has a genuine second session in the seed source — "Supercharge Your SDLC: How AI Agents are Revolutionizing..." at accepted-index 32. You do not need to invent a speaker or a talk. Widening the agenda window past index 32, or promoting that single session into the scheduled set, produces a real two-session speaker from the real 2025 program, which is exactly the fidelity the seed is built for.

Check the geometry before you commit to it, because I have NOT verified this half and you should not take it from me. Under agenda.ts's starts[] construction, index 6 falls in the index 4..8 band (day three 17:00, room ROOM_IDS[6], the workshop-parallel branch) and index 32 would fall in the 18:00+ band at 18 + floor((32-9)/5) = 22:00 on day three, room ROOM_IDS[32 % 4] = ROOM_IDS[0]. Same day, different times, different rooms — which is the sequence you need. What I have NOT established is whether those two rooms sit in DIFFERENT BUILDINGS, and that is the whole point of the strip's walk leg. Resolve ROOM_IDS to buildings and confirm before you build on it. If they share a building you get a room-change with no walk, which exercises less than half the feature.

And whichever route you take, make check:seed fail if that speaker stops having two scheduled sessions in two buildings — same discipline as MRQ-62's Transit fix. A seeded case nothing guards is one refactor from being inert again.

Keep the earlier comment's other half, which is unaffected and independently verified: the two conflict pairs DO give you a person with two sessions at the same instant in two different buildings (the first pair crosses Sheraton to Marriott deliberately), so AC-6's duplicate-DOM-id case reproduces against real seeded data. Also still open and still worth checking first: the conflict participation is seeded with role "moderator", so confirm the portal's submission list includes moderator participations before building on it.

CORRECTION TO MY GATE-DISCIPLINE COMMENT ABOVE, and it lands squarely on this ticket's own seed work. Two parts: a rule I banked too globally, and a mechanism you must understand before you touch check:seed.

PART 1 — THE RED RULE IS PER-SCRIPT, NOT GLOBAL.

I wrote above: "If a gate is RED, BELIEVE IT — status 'fail' is load-invariant." That is true only where status is derived from test OUTCOMES or FINDINGS. It is false where status is a stopwatch, and check:seed — the very gate this ticket asks you to extend — is a stopwatch.

  scripts/checks/check-seed.mjs
    const budgetMs = 30_000;
    status: elapsedMs <= budgetMs ? "pass" : "fail",
    if (result.status === "fail") process.exitCode = 1;

No warn tier, no hard-limit split. Slowness IS a red there, the opposite of run-test.mjs and pr-gate.mjs. And the margin is nothing: it has measured 29638ms against the 30000ms budget (362ms of headroom) and 31142ms on another branch. On a loaded box it is a coin flip. Most of that 30s is withLocalRuntime booting wrangler, not your seed.

The corrected rule, which supersedes what I wrote above:

  Before believing a red, check how THAT script computes status.
  - Status from outcomes/findings -> load-invariant. Believe it. (check-clocks, check-repo,
    check-routes, check-schema, check-shell-truth, check-deploy, trace-ac, verify-design-contract)
  - Status from wall clock -> a red can be pure contention. Re-run under the lock and read
    elapsedMs against budgetMs BEFORE touching code. (check:seed; also check:speed, where it
    is by design because product speed is a graded feature — R7 — but still load-sensitive locally.)
  - run-test / pr-gate -> "fail" is real, "pass-over-budget" is a warn, "timeout" is unknown.

pr-gate does NOT invoke check:seed (verified: no seed reference in pr-gate.mjs), so you will only meet this when you run check:seed directly — which this ticket requires you to do.

PART 2 — THE PART THAT ACTUALLY CHANGES YOUR IMPLEMENTATION.

This ticket says check:seed must fail if the two-session speaker stops existing. Do NOT implement that by setting or influencing the status field. Status is computed from elapsed time alone and ignores findings entirely — a seed defect that runs fast would still report "pass".

check-seed.mjs has TWO INDEPENDENT FAILURE CHANNELS with opposite semantics, and both surface as a non-zero exit:

  1. assert.ok(...) from node:assert/strict, at module top level (see lines ~32-39, e.g.
     "seed must produce a live Transit conflict"). A failed assertion THROWS, the script
     dies, exit is non-zero. This is the real-defect channel and it is load-invariant.
  2. status "fail" from elapsedMs > budgetMs, which sets process.exitCode = 1. This is the
     contention channel.

So: add your speaker assertion to the assert.ok block, alongside the existing Transit-conflict assertion, in exactly that style. That is how MRQ-62's Transit guard works and it is the channel that actually protects a seeded case.

AND HERE IS THE DISCRIMINATOR when check:seed goes red on you, which follows from the two channels:

  - AssertionError with a stack, and NO report written at artifacts/checks/seed.json
      -> a real seed defect. Your assertion fired. Believe it, fix the seed.
  - A clean report at artifacts/checks/seed.json with status "fail" and elapsedMs over 30000,
      every assertion having passed
      -> you were timed out, not broken. Re-run under the gate lock.

Read the report file before you conclude anything. The two failures look identical from the exit code and completely different one level down.

WORTH KNOWING, NOT YOURS TO FIX: the merge captain has asked the intake agent to mint a ticket for "no check script may red on wall clock alone" — check:seed should get the warn tier run-test already has. If that ticket has landed by the time you pick this up, this whole discriminator may be obsolete; check first. If it has not, do not fix it inside this ticket — add your assertion in the existing style and note the sharp edge in your PR body.

This is the same shape as the merge guard keyed on a string that matched its own documentation, and as the amended contract test that asserted labels instead of behaviour: a check whose PASS does not mean what a reader assumes it means. When you add a guard here, make sure it fails for the reason you intend, and prove it — break the seed deliberately, watch the assertion fire, then put it back.

SECOND CORRECTION TO THE SEED FINDING — and this time the CONCLUSION was wrong, not just the reasoning. I executed the seed instead of reading it. Use these numbers; ignore both earlier versions.

WHAT I SAID TWICE: "no speaker has two scheduled sessions", derived by reading — repeat speakers in the source JSON, their accepted-order indices, and agenda.ts's accepted.slice(0, 24).

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. I built the demo seed rows in memory via buildDemoSeedRows() and queried the generated agenda_items, participations, rooms and buildings directly:

  agenda_items: 25          participations: 1025        people: 1102
  people with >= 1 scheduled session:                   29
  people with >= 2 scheduled sessions:                   3
  of those, at DIFFERENT times (a real sequence):        1
  of those, across DIFFERENT buildings:                  0

  Beyang Liu — 2 scheduled, SAME building
      2026-10-13T18:30:00Z   Sheraton New York Times Square   (co_speaker)
      2026-10-13T19:00:00Z   Sheraton New York Times Square   (speaker)

SO THE MULTI-SESSION CASE IS ALREADY REACHABLE. A speaker with two sequential scheduled sessions exists in the seed today. The day strip WILL render for Beyang Liu, in time order, with a room change between 18:30 and 19:00.

WHY MY READING MISSED IT, and it is worth knowing because the same trap is waiting in this ticket. I counted Beyang Liu's appearances as a NAMED SPEAKER in the source program (indices 6 and 32, the second outside the 24-item window) and concluded one scheduled session. But he also holds a CO_SPEAKER participation on another session that IS inside the window. That participation is positional and inherited — it comes from a slot's position in a list, and the schedule is inherited from the session, not named anywhere I could grep. No pattern over the source JSON or the seed scripts would have found it. Only executing the seed did.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING IS NARROWER AND MORE PRECISE THAN I TOLD YOU:

  NOT missing:  a speaker with two scheduled sessions          (Beyang Liu has it)
  NOT missing:  a sequence at different times                  (18:30 -> 19:00)
  MISSING:      any speaker whose two sessions are in DIFFERENT BUILDINGS   (0 of 3)

So the walk leg — the one thing the strip exists to say, and the only part that exercises arrivalForSession's cross-building geometry — is unreachable, while everything around it works. That is a smaller and much cheaper fix than "seed a two-talk speaker": move ONE of Beyang Liu's two sessions into a different pinned building, or schedule an existing cross-building pair onto one person. His 18:30/19:00 pair is 30 minutes apart, which is tight for a real walk, so check that whatever you choose still produces a sensible leave_by rather than a negative one.

Beware also: with both sessions 30 minutes apart and the first's duration unknown to me, previousSessionFor() only matches a prior session that ENDS at or before the next one starts. If the 18:30 session runs longer than 30 minutes, it is not the previous session of the 19:00 one and NO leg is computed at all — the two would render as an overlap, not a sequence. Verify that against the real durations before assuming the sequence case is exercised.

AND MAKE check:seed GUARD THE CROSS-BUILDING PAIR SPECIFICALLY, not merely "a speaker with two sessions" — that assertion passes today and would protect nothing. Add it to the assert.ok block in scripts/checks/check-seed.mjs alongside the Transit-conflict assertion, since that file's status field is a stopwatch and ignores findings entirely.

METHOD NOTE, because it is the reusable part. Both earlier versions of this finding were derived by reading source. The coupling that falsified them was POSITIONAL and INHERITED — a co-speaker slot's index, and a schedule inherited from a session — and it is invisible to any grep by construction, not by carelessness. A search is sound for NAMED references and blind to positional, ordinal and inherited ones. When the dependency could be an index, a slice, a default, a sort order or an insertion sequence, execute the thing and query the result; do not read it. The probe that settled this was about forty lines and ran in a second.
